docs.text: LPJ-GUESS DAVE DAVE ( D ynamics of A ustralian VE getation) is a fork of LPJ-GUESS, a dynamic global vegetation model (DGVM), used for simulating Australian ecosystems. This documentation site is the central reference for running, developing, and understanding the DAVE fork. What you'll find here Science documentation for model behaviour and process details. How-to guides for setup and execution workflows. Project context for developers working on the DAVE codebase. Scope of this docs site The docs focus on the DAVE fork and workflows commonly used in this repository (including OzFlux site simulations and debugging/development workflows). As the site grows, additional pages for Linux/macOS setup, run configuration, outputs, and developer internals will be added under the existing sections.

docs.text: Contributing Code (Policy) This page defines governance and quality expectations for code contributions. For step-by-step contributor workflow, see Contributing Code (Workflow) . For command-level Git instructions, see: Version Control via CLI Version Control via SourceTree 1. Roles and Permissions Maintainers (ie Drew) Maintain this fork and its protected branches. Sync changes from the upstream LPJ-GUESS repository. Review and merge Merge Requests (MRs). Curate the overall structure of long-lived development branches. Developers (ie postdocs) Implement new features and fixes. Work primarily on long-lived personal branches in this team repository. Open MRs from long-lived branches back to lpjguess_dave . Reporters (ie students) Run the model and test results. Report bugs and issues. Review documentation and suggest improvements. Optional: contribute code via branches (with guidance from a maintainer). 2. Branch and Repository Policy Protected branches lpjguess_dave : primary, stable branch for team work. All merges require MR and review. trunk : tracking branch for upstream LPJ-GUESS. Maintainers only. Long-lived personal branches Naming convention: lpjguess_dave_<name> lpjguess_dave_<name>_<short-topic> (optional qualifier) Examples: lpjguess_dave_clare lpjguess_dave_juergen_adaptive Policy: Long-lived branches live in this team repository (not personal forks). They remain the primary working branch for each developer. They are not deleted after merges to lpjguess_dave . Short-lived feature branches Use for risky or isolated work. Merge into either the relevant long-lived branch or directly into lpjguess_dave . Delete after merge. 3. Upstream Sync Policy (Maintainers) Maintainers periodically sync from upstream LPJ-GUESS to trunk , then open an MR from trunk to lpjguess_dave . After this integration, developers should update their own long-lived branches. 4. MR Quality Expectations All MRs targeting lpjguess_dave should include: What changed. Why it changed (scientific or technical motivation). How it was tested (runs/configs/checks). Expected impact on model outputs, where relevant. Keep commits and MRs focused; prefer smaller reviewable changes. 5. Issues and Bug Reporting Use GitLab Issues for: Bugs Performance problems Documentation gaps Feature requests Include: Clear description Reproduction steps Expected vs actual behaviour Relevant input files/logs Branch context ( lpjguess_dave , lpjguess_dave_<name> , etc.) 6. Code and Scientific Documentation Practices Write clear, readable code. Comment non-obvious logic or scientific assumptions. Document important equations and references in code comments or Markdown. Highlight output-impacting changes in MR descriptions. Before merge to lpjguess_dave , ensure code compiles/runs and outputs pass sanity checks appropriate to the change.

docs.text: LPJ-GUESS Development Ecosystem This page provides a high-level overview of how LPJ-GUESS development is organised across version-control systems and teams, and where DAVE now fits. Primary development systems LPJ-GUESS development primarily occurs in SVN , on a server hosted by the Lund team. A large part of the LPJ-GUESS community still works exclusively in SVN, and many contributors do not use Git in day-to-day workflows. In parallel, the core team maintains a self-hosted GitLab server that mirrors trunk and several key branches from the SVN server. Typical Git workflow in the LPJ-GUESS community Among Git users, the common workflow has historically been SVN-like: Each developer maintains their own branch on the main shared Git repository. Development happens primarily on those per-user branches. Collaboration occurs by coordinating changes across those branches. DAVE historical workflow The DAVE team previously followed this same model, with roughly a dozen DAVE branches on the shared upstream Git repository. DAVE current workflow DAVE has now moved to a fork-based workflow : A dedicated DAVE fork has been created. Going forward, all DAVE development is intended to occur on this fork. The DAVE documentation website is also maintained in this fork under docs/ . Practical implication When discussing development workflow for DAVE, this fork should be treated as the canonical development home, while recognising that the broader LPJ-GUESS ecosystem remains anchored in SVN and mirrored into GitLab.

docs.text: Dependencies and Toolchains This page describes the build system, compilers, and library dependencies used to compile LPJ-GUESS DAVE. It is intended as an orientation for developers rather than a step-by-step setup reference — see the platform setup guides for the latter. Build System DAVE (and LPJ-GUESS more broadly) uses CMake . CMake generates native build files (Makefiles on Unix-like systems, Ninja files, or IDE project files) from a platform-independent description. All compiler and dependency detection happens at the CMake configure step. All external library dependencies are detected automatically and are optional at the CMake level — the project will configure and compile without any of them, but certain features will be disabled. The CMake output will report which dependencies were found. Compilers The following compilers are supported: Platform Compiler Notes Linux GCC Primary development target macOS Clang (via Xcode) Exposed as gcc by the Xcode Command Line Tools Windows MinGW-w64 (GCC) Installed via MSYS2; the recommended Windows toolchain Windows MSVC Technically supported but not extensively tested Library Dependencies NetCDF (practically required) The NetCDF-C library is required to read NetCDF input files. Since all standard DAVE simulation workflows (OzFlux site-level and beyond) use NetCDF-format climate forcing data, the model is not useful in practice without this dependency. ZLIB (optional) If ZLIB is found, output file compression is enabled automatically. This is a minor convenience feature and has no effect on science outputs. MPI (optional) If an MPI implementation is found on Unix-like systems, MPI support is compiled in, enabling parallel job submission workflows. MPI is not needed for single-core development or debugging runs. Platform Setup Guides For installation instructions on your specific platform: Windows macOS Linux

docs.text: Linux Setup Guide This guide covers how to set up and compile LPJ-GUESS DAVE on Linux. After completing this setup, follow Running and Debugging via VSCode to run a site simulation. Dependencies On Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install cmake g++ libnetcdf-dev On other distributions, install the equivalent packages via your native package manager. You need: A C++ compiler (GCC or Clang) CMake NetCDF-C development headers and library Visual Studio Code (optional) VSCode is recommended for interactive debugging (though not strictly required). Download it from the official website , then install the following extensions ( Ctrl+Shift+X ): C/C++ — language support and IntelliSense CodeLLDB — debugger integration Command Variable — used by the run/debug launch configurations to prompt for input Obtaining Source Code Clone the DAVE repository: git clone git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Or via HTTPS: git clone https://stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se/dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Compilation From the repository root: cmake -B build -S . cmake --build build The compiled binary will be at build/guess . Next Step: Run the Model Download the OzFlux forcing data from HIE-Storage , then follow Running and Debugging via VSCode to run the CumberlandPlain site and check the output files.

docs.text: macOS Setup Guide This guide covers how to set up and compile LPJ-GUESS DAVE on macOS using the Clang/Apple toolchain and VSCode. After completing this setup, follow Running and Debugging via VSCode to run a site simulation. Software Installation Many setup steps use Terminal. To open Terminal, press Cmd+Space , type Terminal , and press Enter. When this guide says to run a command, paste it into Terminal and press Enter. Xcode Command Line Tools The Xcode Command Line Tools provide the compiler (clang, which masquerades as gcc) and other essential build utilities. To check whether they are already installed, run: gcc --version If they are not installed, you will see a dialog prompting you to install them. You can also trigger this manually: xcode-select --install Homebrew Homebrew is a package manager for macOS used to install the remaining dependencies. To check if it is already installed: brew --version If it is not installed, follow the instructions at brew.sh . Dependencies Install CMake and NetCDF via Homebrew: brew install cmake netcdf Visual Studio Code Download and install VSCode from the official website . Once installed, open the Extensions panel ( Cmd+Shift+X ) and install the following extensions: C/C++ — language support and IntelliSense CodeLLDB — debugger integration (uses lldb under the hood) Command Variable — used by the run/debug launch configurations to prompt for input Obtaining Source Code Clone the DAVE repository: git clone git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Or via HTTPS if you have not set up an SSH key: git clone https://stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se/dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Compilation From the repository root: cmake -B build -S . cmake --build build The compiled binary will be at build/guess . Next Step: Run the Model Download the OzFlux forcing data from HIE-Storage , then follow Running and Debugging via VSCode to run the CumberlandPlain site and check the output files.

docs.text: LPJ-GUESS DAVE Windows Setup Guide Preamble This guide explains how to compile, run, and debug LPJ-GUESS DAVE on windows, using the msys2 toolchain + vscode. It's possible to instead use Microsoft compilers (MSVC) and visual studio, and while that will work, it's beyond the scope of this guide (ie: you're on your own). Software Installation Download and install filezilla Download and install sourcetree (skip bitbucket config, disable mercurial) Download and install visual studio code (not visual studio) Download and install msys2 (I recommend using the default installation path) Software Configuration/Setup MSYS2 Run the following command from inside msys2: pacman -S mingw-w64-x86_64-{gcc,cmake,netcdf,gdb,make,ninja} Update PATH to include MinGW64 Go to the start menu and search for "environment", and click on "Edit environment variables for the current user". Double click on "Path", then click "New". Here you will need to use the path into which you installed msys2. By default this was C:\msys64 , but if you installed it in a different location, use that location instead. Add the following path: C:\path\to\msys64\mingw64\bin . E.g. for the default installation options: C:\msys64\mingw64\bin . Click OK to save the changes, and click OK on the environment variables window as well. To make sure this worked, open a new command prompt and run gcc . If you get a "command not found" error, then something has gone wrong - talk to Drew. If you get something like "fatal error: no input files", then you're all set. If Visual Studio Code is installed and running, close it and reopen it. SSH Key Generation DO NOT do this if you already have a key. To check if you have a key, navigate to C:\Users\username\.ssh . If this directory doesn't exist, you don't have a key. If you have a file in here called something like id_ed25519 , id_rsa , etc, then you already have an SSH key. Never overwrite this key unless you know what you're doing. If you don't have an SSH key, open a command prompt and run the following command: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 Just click "enter" at each prompt to generate a key with the default name and without a passphrase. Your key file comes in two parts, stored as two separate files in the C:\Users\username\.ssh directory: id_ed25519 ( Private key ) id_ed25519.pub ( Public key ) In windows, it can be difficult to distinguish between the two files, so it can be useful to enable the display of file path extensions in windows explorer. GitLab Account If you don't already have a gitlab account, navigate to the Lund Gitlab in a browser and create one. GitLab SSH Key Go to your preferences page in gitlab, and click "SSH Keys" on the left, click "Add new key". Copy the contents of your public key ( C:\Users\username\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub ) and add it to your GitLab account. Make sure you copy the file ending with .pub, which is your public key, as opposed to the file with the same name but no file extension, which is your private key and should be treated like a password (ie not shared with anyone). To get the contents of your public key, you can open it in a text editor such as notepad, or print it from a command prompt (e.g. type C:\Users\username\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub ) FileZilla Go to the site manager (top-left, beneath the "file" button). Click "New site" to register a new server with the following details: Protocol: SFTP - SSH File Transfer Protocol Host: hie-storage.sstars.ws Port: leave empty Logon Type: Key file User: Your hie-storage username (e.g. u90123456) Key file: Your private key (e.g. C:\Users\username\.ssh\id_ed25519 ) Click OK to save this server configuration. To later connect to hie-storage, select this server from the drop-down list to the right of the "site manager" button. Visual Studio Code Open Visual Studio Code, hit ctrl+shift+x to open the extension manager, and install the following extensions: C++ Native Debug Obtaining Source Code Open SourceTree and click "clone". Use the following details: Remote URL: git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:DAVE/LPJ-GUESS-DAVE.git Destination Path: C:\some\path\on\your\computer The code will be downloaded into the destination path, so choose wherever works best for you. Obtaining Climate Data Climate data must be downloaded from hie-storage. If you don't have an account, talk to Drew. On hie-storage, the following directory must be downloaded: /data/hiestorage/WorkingData/MEDLYN_GROUP/PROJECTS/dynamics_simulations/lpj-guess/forcing/ozflux/processed This directory must be downloaded into your source code directory, inside <source code directory>\benchmarks\ozflux , and it must be renamed to forcing. So you should end up with a directory named <source code directory>\benchmarks\ozflux\forcing\met . Next Step: Run the Model After completing the Windows setup, follow Running and Debugging via VSCode to run the CumberlandPlain site and check that outputs are being produced. Configuring the Model This section could be arbitrarily long, so here I will briefly describe the input file tree and list the main areas of interest. For navigating these files, I recommend using the Visual Studio Code builtin file explorer (top button in the left-hand sidebar, above run and debug, or use the keyboard shortcut "ctrl+shift+e"). Alternatively, if you want to go to a specific file, use the keyboard shortcut "ctrl+p", type the file name, and hit enter. All of the input files related to the ozflux sites are in the benchmarks\ozflux directory. In here is one directory for each site. Each site-level directory contains its own instruction file, named <site>.ins . These site-level .ins files are very short but import other instruction files from the ozflux directory, which contain the parameters common to all sites: settings.ins : Contains most top-level switches, and, near the bottom of the file, controls at a high level which kinds of PFTs are included in the simulation. outputs.ins : Contains all available output files which can be generated by the model, most of which are disabled by default. To enable or disable an output, simply comment/uncomment it. The comment character is an exclamation mark (!). trees.ins : Contains parameters for all tree PFTs, as well as fine-grained control over which specific trees are included in the simulation. c3g.ins : Contains parameters for all C3 grass PFTs. c4g.ins : Contains parameters for all C4 grass PFTs. pft_common.ins : Contains parameters common to all PFTs.

docs.text: DO NOT do this if you already have a key. To check if you have a key, navigate to C:\Users\username\.ssh . If this directory doesn't exist, you don't have a key. If you have a file in here called something like id_ed25519 , id_rsa , etc, then you already have an SSH key. Never overwrite this key unless you know what you're doing. If you don't have an SSH key, open a command prompt and run the following command: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 Just click "enter" at each prompt to generate a key with the default name and without a passphrase. Your key file comes in two parts, stored as two separate files in the C:\Users\username\.ssh directory: id_ed25519 ( Private key ) id_ed25519.pub ( Public key ) In windows, it can be difficult to distinguish between the two files, so it can be useful to enable the display of file path extensions in windows explorer.
docs.title: SSH Key Generation

docs.text: If you don't already have a gitlab account, navigate to the Lund Gitlab in a browser and create one.
docs.title: GitLab Account

docs.text: Go to your preferences page in gitlab, and click "SSH Keys" on the left, click "Add new key". Copy the contents of your public key ( C:\Users\username\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub ) and add it to your GitLab account. Make sure you copy the file ending with .pub, which is your public key, as opposed to the file with the same name but no file extension, which is your private key and should be treated like a password (ie not shared with anyone). To get the contents of your public key, you can open it in a text editor such as notepad, or print it from a command prompt (e.g. type C:\Users\username\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub )

docs.text: This section could be arbitrarily long, so here I will briefly describe the input file tree and list the main areas of interest. For navigating these files, I recommend using the Visual Studio Code builtin file explorer (top button in the left-hand sidebar, above run and debug, or use the keyboard shortcut "ctrl+shift+e"). Alternatively, if you want to go to a specific file, use the keyboard shortcut "ctrl+p", type the file name, and hit enter. All of the input files related to the ozflux sites are in the benchmarks\ozflux directory. In here is one directory for each site. Each site-level directory contains its own instruction file, named <site>.ins . These site-level .ins files are very short but import other instruction files from the ozflux directory, which contain the parameters common to all sites: settings.ins : Contains most top-level switches, and, near the bottom of the file, controls at a high level which kinds of PFTs are included in the simulation. outputs.ins : Contains all available output files which can be generated by the model, most of which are disabled by default. To enable or disable an output, simply comment/uncomment it. The comment character is an exclamation mark (!). trees.ins : Contains parameters for all tree PFTs, as well as fine-grained control over which specific trees are included in the simulation. c3g.ins : Contains parameters for all C3 grass PFTs. c4g.ins : Contains parameters for all C4 grass PFTs. pft_common.ins : Contains parameters common to all PFTs.

docs.text: Climate Input The DAVE input module is the standard input module for DAVE simulations. It reads subdaily, CF-compliant NetCDF forcing data into LPJ-GUESS. Background The DAVE climate input stack is loosely based on the cf input module used by upstream LPJ-GUESS, but adds support for subdaily meteorological inputs . Subdaily inputs are required by the DAVE photosynthesis module , which operates at sub-daily time resolution. Input Architecture At a high level: DAVEInput is the top-level input module selected by -input nc . NCInput is the climate-specific submodule used by DAVEInput . NCInput discovers required variables from NetCDF metadata ( standard_name units ) and reads the corresponding timeseries. Selecting the Module Pass -input nc on the command line: ./build/guess -input nc myfile.ins Or in the context of a parallel run: mpirun -np 8 ./build/guess -parallel -input nc <insfile> nc is the current CLI key for DAVE climate input. A future breaking release may introduce dave as the module key. Instruction File Parameters All parameters are declared in modules/daveinput.cpp . Parameters with no default listed are required and must be set explicitly. Simulation resolution Parameter Type Range Default Description nsteps_day int 1–86400 — Number of subdaily timesteps per day (e.g. 48 for half-hourly) Input file paths Parameter Type Default Description file_met_forcing string — Path or shell-glob pattern for CF-compliant NetCDF met forcing files file_met_spinup string (same as forcing) Path or shell-glob pattern for NetCDF met data used during spinup. If omitted, file_met_forcing is used for both spinup and simulation. file_gridlist string — Path to gridlist file (one lon lat pair per line) file_soildata string — Path to soil input file file_ndep string — Path to nitrogen deposition archive file (used when N deposition is not read from NetCDF variables) file_co2 string — Path to annual CO₂ text file (format: year ppm , one row per year). Used when CO₂ is not read from NetCDF file_thome string — Path to mean maximum temperature ( \(T_{home}\) ) input file. Required when iftempacclimation is enabled. Humidity method If humidity is provided as relative humidity (rather than direct VPD), specify the saturation vapour pressure method: Parameter Type Options Description esat_method string sonntag_1990 , alduchov_1996 , allen_1998 Method for computing saturation vapour pressure from temperature Atmospheric pressure Parameter Type Range Description fixed_pressure float 0–200000 Fixed constant atmospheric pressure to use (Pa). Default: 0 (disabled). CO₂ concentration Parameter Type Description file_co2 string Path to a text file of annual CO₂ values (see above). If omitted, CO₂ may be read from NetCDF where present. Parameter Type Default Description use_mean_annual_co2 bool false If true, each timestep uses the annual mean CO₂; otherwise the subdaily values from the file are averaged per day Nitrogen deposition Parameter Type Options Description ndep_scenario string HISTORIC , RCP26 , RCP45 , RCP60 , RCP85 Scenario for the nitrogen deposition archive ( file_ndep ) Spinup Parameter Type Range Default Description spinup_met_cycle_length int 0–1000000 0 Number of years of met data to draw from during spinup. 0 means all available years are used. Perturbations These add a constant offset to the corresponding variable at every timestep. Useful for sensitivity experiments. Parameter Type Range Default Description temperature_delta float 0–1×10⁶ 0 Offset added to temperature at every timestep (°C) co2_delta float 0–1×10⁶ 0 Offset added to CO₂ at every timestep (ppm) Performance and diagnostics Parameter Type Default Description cache_strategy int (0–2) — Caching strategy: 0 = cache entire file (fastest, highest memory), 1 = cache one year at a time (recommended for large files), 2 = no caching (slowest) nc_check_inputs bool — If enabled, performs sanity checks on met values at each timestep progress_interval int -1 Interval in seconds between progress log lines. 0 = yearly; -1 = daily progress_newline bool false Terminate progress messages with a newline (recommended for MPI runs) strict_math bool — Treat invalid floating-point operations (e.g. division by zero) as fatal errors NetCDF Variable Discovery and Metadata Requirements NCInput discovers variables from NetCDF metadata. For each variable it uses, the NetCDF variable must include: standard_name units Variables without both attributes are ignored by the resolver. Required coordinate metadata Coordinate variables must be discoverable with these standard_name values: longitude latitude time The time coordinate must also include CF-compatible units (for example days since 1850-01-01 ) and calendar . Climate variables and accepted standard_name values The table below lists the names currently recognised by DAVE climate input. Input quantity standard_name values Air temperature (required) air_temperature Shortwave radiation (required) surface_downwelling_shortwave_flux_in_air , surface_downwelling_shortwave_flux Precipitation (required) thickness_of_rainfall_amount , precipitation_amount , precipitation_flux Humidity (one required source) VPD: water_vapor_saturation_deficit_in_air or water_vapor_saturation_deficit ; OR relative humidity: relative_humidity ; OR specific humidity: specific_humidity Surface pressure (required unless fixed_pressure > 0) surface_air_pressure CO₂ (required if file_co2 not provided) mole_fraction_of_carbon_dioxide_in_air Wind speed (required when BLAZE is enabled) wind_speed Daily Tmax/Tmin (required for daily forcing with BLAZE) maximum_air_temperature , minimum_air_temperature NetCDF N deposition (optional alternative to archive input) ndep_nhx , ndep_noy Units Units are validated when climate variables are opened. In practice, datasets should use these units: Temperature: degC / °C / ℃ Shortwave radiation: W/m2 or W m-2 Precipitation: mm , kg m-2 , or kg/m2 VPD: kPa Relative humidity: 1 Specific humidity: 1 or kg/kg Pressure: Pa CO₂: ppm Wind speed: m/s or m s-1 NetCDF N deposition: kgN/m2/day Uniqueness rule Within a resolved input set, each required standard_name must map to a single variable. Ambiguous duplicates for the same standard_name are treated as an error. Spinup Climate Cycling During spinup (the first nyear_spinup years), the module maps each spinup year to a calendar year of met data by cycling deterministically through the available years. Only complete calendar years are used for simulation. If a NetCDF file starts partway through a year, that first partial year is skipped; if it ends partway through a year, that final partial year is skipped. The goal is for the met years used in spinup to align with the transition into the main simulation period. When a separate spinup file is used, the usable spinup period ends at the earlier of: the last complete year in file_met_spinup , and the year immediately before the first complete year in file_met_forcing . Any overlap in file_met_spinup after the main forcing begins is ignored for the final spinup cycle and for the main simulation. How years are selected The module cycles through the spinup dataset in order, wrapping back to the start when it reaches the end. The cycling is deterministic — the same run configuration always produces the same sequence. The wrap-around point is chosen so that the sequence ends at the transition into the main forcing. Once the calendar year falls within the usable spinup range, actual data years are used directly with no cycling. Example — suppose the spinup dataset covers 1990–1999 (10 years), the spinup runs for 30 years, and the main simulation begins in 2000: Spinup year Calendar year Met data year 0 1970 1990 cycling begins 1 1971 1991 ... ... ... 8 1978 1998 9 1979 1999 end of cycle 1 10 1980 1990 cycle 2 begins 11 1981 1991 ... ... ... 19 1989 1999 end of cycle 2 20 1990 1990 within data range — direct ... ... ... 28 1998 1998 29 1999 1999 last spinup year — 2000 2000 simulation begins The data cycles twice, and the transition into the simulation data at year 2000 occurs naturally at the end of the final cycle year. If the spinup file overlaps the main forcing, the transition still occurs at the first complete year in file_met_forcing . For example, if file_met_spinup contains complete years 1900-2010 and file_met_forcing contains complete years 2001-2100, the final spinup cycle uses 1900-2000 from the spinup file, and the main forcing is used from 2001 onward. The overlapping spinup years 2001-2010 are not used. If spinup_met_cycle_length is set to a value greater than zero, only the first N years of the spinup dataset are used for cycling. This is useful when only a short pre-industrial baseline period should be repeated during spinup, even if a longer dataset is available. CO₂ is not cycled CO₂ concentration is always taken from the actual calendar year being simulated. It is not cycled with the meteorology, even during spinup. Separate spinup file A separate NetCDF file can be specified via file_met_spinup for the spinup period. This is useful when a longer historical baseline record exists (e.g. a reanalysis product covering a pre-industrial period) that differs from the main simulation forcing. If file_met_spinup is not set, or is identical to file_met_forcing , the same file is used for both periods. When a separate spinup file is used, the module opens the spinup file first, determines the available years and timestep, and then switches to the main forcing file at the first complete year available in the main forcing data. The spinup file must contain at least one complete year before that first main forcing year. A spinup file that starts in or after the main forcing period is not supported. Multi-file Input Paths file_met_forcing and file_met_spinup accept either: a single NetCDF path, or a shell-glob pattern ( * and ? ) that resolves to multiple NetCDF files. Examples: file_met_forcing "/data/barra2/forcing_*.nc" file_met_spinup "/data/barra2/spinup_19??.nc" Matched files are sorted and then scanned for variables using metadata resolution ( standard_name + units ). NetCDF Input Format Input files must follow CF Conventions 1.6 : A time coordinate variable with units (e.g. "days since 1850-01-01" ) and calendar attributes. Coordinate variables with standard_name values longitude , latitude , and time . scale_factor / add_offset and missing_value attributes are not supported. The input timestep (steps/day in the forcing files) must be greater than or equal to nsteps_day and must be an integer multiple of nsteps_day . For example, 48 input steps/day can be aggregated to 24 requested steps/day.

docs.text: Common Failures This page lists common failures, and what to do about them. For the local VSCode workflow, see Running and Debugging via VSCode . First: Did the Run Complete? When the model finishes normally, the terminal ends with text like: Simulation completed in 15.05 seconds with 0 errors and 0 warnings. See guess.log for full details Finished The time and counts will differ. A completed run can have warnings, and some model configurations may report non-fatal errors; Simulation completed means the model finished the simulation successfully and wrote outputs. If the terminal instead contains: FATAL ERROR: ... Simulation terminated. the run failed. Read the first line after FATAL ERROR: ; it is usually the useful part. In VSCode on Windows or Linux, open the Terminal panel at the bottom of the window and scroll up if needed. On macOS, open Debug Console from the panel dropdown instead. Whether the run completed or failed, the full log is in the site's directory. For Cumberland Plain it is: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/guess.log Open this file in VSCode, then use Ctrl+F (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+F (macOS) to search for FATAL , ERROR , or a distinctive word from the terminal message. See Running and Debugging via VSCode for where outputs and logs are created. Where supported by the build platform, the log also includes a stack trace after a fatal error; this is mainly useful when reporting the problem to a developer. Couldn't find input module nc Typical terminal text: Couldn't find input module nc The executable was built without NetCDF support. The OzFlux simulations use NetCDF climate forcing, and nc is the DAVE input module supplied only when NetCDF was found during configuration. Install NetCDF using the setup instructions for your platform, then configure and build again from the repository root. Do not only rerun the build command: the configuration step must be repeated so that CMake can find NetCDF. Windows setup macOS setup Linux setup cmake -B build -S . cmake --build build NetCDF error: ... Cannot open NetCDF file: ... Typical terminal or log text: NetCDF error: No such file or directory: Cannot open NetCDF file: ../forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc The path at the end is the file the model could not find. For the standard Cumberland Plain run, check that this exact file exists: benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc If it is absent, download the full OzFlux forcing directory and place it as benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/ ; the guide explains the expected location and transfer options: HIE-Storage . If the file exists but the error still names a path beginning ../forcing/ , run the model from the site directory. The command-line steps are in Running Serially . VSCode's supplied run configurations choose the site directory automatically; see Running and Debugging via VSCode . Error: could not open ... for input Typical terminal or log text: Error: could not open CumberlandPlain.ins for input or: Failed to open gridlist file: gridlist.txt The model cannot find an instruction or supporting input file. First check the name in the message for a typo. Then check where the command was run: for an OzFlux site, the current directory should be that site's folder, for example: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/ The site instruction files deliberately use relative paths. Running Serially explains this convention, and OzFlux Site Simulations describes the files that a site imports. Error: Path does not match any files: ... Typical terminal or log text: Error: Path does not match any files: '../forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc' This has the same practical meaning as a missing input file: inspect the path in the message, confirm that the file is present, and make sure the model was started from the site directory. Follow the checks in NetCDF error: ... Cannot open NetCDF file: ... . cmake: command not found , cmake is not recognised , or a Compiler Is Missing Typical terminal text includes one of: cmake: command not found 'cmake' is not recognized as an internal or external command gcc: command not found The build tools are not installed, or the terminal/VSCode was opened before they were added to the system path. Return to the appropriate platform setup guide, complete its dependency instructions, then close and reopen the terminal and VSCode before trying again. Windows setup macOS setup Linux setup The Run Configuration Is Missing in VSCode Symptoms: The Run and Debug panel does not offer an OzFlux site such as CumberlandPlain . Pressing F5 does not build or run an OzFlux simulation. Open the repository root folder in VSCode, rather than modules/ , benchmarks/ , or an individual site folder. In the Explorer panel, the root should contain benchmarks/ , docs/ , framework/ , modules/ , and .vscode/ . The tracked .vscode/launch.json and .vscode/tasks.json files provide the run configurations. If .vscode/ is absent, update to the expected branch or ask Drew to check the checkout. For the normal VSCode workflow, see Running and Debugging via VSCode . Simulation completed ... but out/ Is Empty or a File Is Missing First confirm that you are looking in the site's own output directory, for example: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/out/ The available outputs are configured in benchmarks/ozflux/outputs.ins . Lines beginning with ! are disabled. For example: file_dave_gpp "dave_gpp.out" !file_dave_gpp "dave_gpp.out" The first line writes dave_gpp.out ; the second does not. See OzFlux Site Simulations for the shared configuration files, and Running and Debugging via VSCode for the usual output locations. The Run Is Still Printing Progress If the terminal continues to update a percentage complete, the model is still running. If spinup_output is enabeld, the outputs will include spinup years and may take noticeably longer in a Debug build. Wait for either the completion text described above or a fatal error before treating the run as finished. For a different way to start a local run, see Running Serially . The guides for PBS jobs on Gadi are separate and are not needed for local site runs. Do not stage them unless a maintainer has specifically asked for them. The Repository Map explains which directories contain generated files and which contain the model inputs or source code. After Updating, Files or Run Configurations Are Missing First check that SourceTree shows the expected branch. If you use the command line, the following shows the current branch and whether local changes need attention: git status Then fetch and pull the expected branch in SourceTree. The project workflow is documented in Version Control via SourceTree and Version Control via CLI . If files are still missing after updating, ask a maintainer to check whether the checkout is sparse, filtered, or incomplete.

docs.text: This page lists common failures, and what to do about them. For the local VSCode workflow, see Running and Debugging via VSCode .
docs.title: Common Failures

docs.text: When the model finishes normally, the terminal ends with text like: Simulation completed in 15.05 seconds with 0 errors and 0 warnings. See guess.log for full details Finished The time and counts will differ. A completed run can have warnings, and some model configurations may report non-fatal errors; Simulation completed means the model finished the simulation successfully and wrote outputs. If the terminal instead contains: FATAL ERROR: ... Simulation terminated. the run failed. Read the first line after FATAL ERROR: ; it is usually the useful part. In VSCode on Windows or Linux, open the Terminal panel at the bottom of the window and scroll up if needed. On macOS, open Debug Console from the panel dropdown instead. Whether the run completed or failed, the full log is in the site's directory. For Cumberland Plain it is: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/guess.log Open this file in VSCode, then use Ctrl+F (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+F (macOS) to search for FATAL , ERROR , or a distinctive word from the terminal message. See Running and Debugging via VSCode for where outputs and logs are created. Where supported by the build platform, the log also includes a stack trace after a fatal error; this is mainly useful when reporting the problem to a developer.
docs.title: First: Did the Run Complete?

docs.text: Typical terminal text: Couldn't find input module nc The executable was built without NetCDF support. The OzFlux simulations use NetCDF climate forcing, and nc is the DAVE input module supplied only when NetCDF was found during configuration. Install NetCDF using the setup instructions for your platform, then configure and build again from the repository root. Do not only rerun the build command: the configuration step must be repeated so that CMake can find NetCDF. Windows setup macOS setup Linux setup cmake -B build -S . cmake --build build
docs.title: Couldn't find input module nc

docs.text: Typical terminal or log text: NetCDF error: No such file or directory: Cannot open NetCDF file: ../forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc The path at the end is the file the model could not find. For the standard Cumberland Plain run, check that this exact file exists: benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc If it is absent, download the full OzFlux forcing directory and place it as benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/ ; the guide explains the expected location and transfer options: HIE-Storage . If the file exists but the error still names a path beginning ../forcing/ , run the model from the site directory. The command-line steps are in Running Serially . VSCode's supplied run configurations choose the site directory automatically; see Running and Debugging via VSCode .
docs.title: NetCDF error: ... Cannot open NetCDF file: ...

docs.text: Typical terminal or log text: Error: could not open CumberlandPlain.ins for input or: Failed to open gridlist file: gridlist.txt The model cannot find an instruction or supporting input file. First check the name in the message for a typo. Then check where the command was run: for an OzFlux site, the current directory should be that site's folder, for example: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/ The site instruction files deliberately use relative paths. Running Serially explains this convention, and OzFlux Site Simulations describes the files that a site imports.
docs.title: Error: could not open ... for input

docs.text: Typical terminal or log text: Error: Path does not match any files: '../forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc' This has the same practical meaning as a missing input file: inspect the path in the message, confirm that the file is present, and make sure the model was started from the site directory. Follow the checks in NetCDF error: ... Cannot open NetCDF file: ... .
docs.title: Error: Path does not match any files: ...

docs.text: Typical terminal text includes one of: cmake: command not found 'cmake' is not recognized as an internal or external command gcc: command not found The build tools are not installed, or the terminal/VSCode was opened before they were added to the system path. Return to the appropriate platform setup guide, complete its dependency instructions, then close and reopen the terminal and VSCode before trying again. Windows setup macOS setup Linux setup
docs.title: cmake: command not found, cmake is not recognised, or a Compiler Is Missing

docs.text: Symptoms: The Run and Debug panel does not offer an OzFlux site such as CumberlandPlain . Pressing F5 does not build or run an OzFlux simulation. Open the repository root folder in VSCode, rather than modules/ , benchmarks/ , or an individual site folder. In the Explorer panel, the root should contain benchmarks/ , docs/ , framework/ , modules/ , and .vscode/ . The tracked .vscode/launch.json and .vscode/tasks.json files provide the run configurations. If .vscode/ is absent, update to the expected branch or ask Drew to check the checkout. docs.text: First confirm that you are looking in the site's own output directory, for example: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/out/ The available outputs are configured in benchmarks/ozflux/outputs.ins . docs.text: Contributing Code (Workflow) This page covers the practical day-to-day workflow for contributing code. For branch policy, roles, and maintainer responsibilities, see Contributing Code (Policy) . If you need UI/terminal-specific Git guidance, see: Version Control via SourceTree Version Control via CLI 1. Getting Started (First-Time Setup) Clone the DAVE team repository and confirm you can authenticate and push. Use either the CLI or SourceTree guides above for exact commands. If you previously worked on the old/core LPJ-GUESS repo , see Migrating from the Old Upstream LPJ-GUESS Repository . 2. Primary Workflow: Long-Lived Personal Branches This is the main workflow for most developers (postdocs). 2.1. Create or update your long-lived branch Make sure your local lpjguess_dave is current, then create or switch to your long-lived branch ( lpjguess_dave_<your_name> ). Periodically bring changes from lpjguess_dave into your long-lived branch. If you are unsure when to merge vs rebase, ask a maintainer. 2.2. Make and commit changes Work as usual in your lpjguess_dave_<your_name> branch and commit focused, logical changes. Keep commits reasonably small and focused where possible. Push regularly so your branch is backed up and ready for review. 2.3. Creating a Merge Request from your dev branch to lpjguess_dave Periodically, when your branch is in a good state to integrate: Ensure your branch is up to date. In GitLab, open a Merge Request : Go to the gitlab repository -> code -> merge requests -> new (or use this link ) Source branch: dave/lpj-guess-dave : lpjguess_dave_<your_name> Target branch: dave/lpj-guess-dave : lpjguess_dave NOTE: The repository (first dropdown) in the target branch defaults to lpj-guess-developers/LPJ-GUESS . This needs to be changed to dave/lpj-guess-dave ; otherwise, the MR will be submitted against the upstream LPJ-GUESS repository. 3. Fill out the MR description: - What the change does - Why it’s needed (scientific or technical motivation) - How you tested it (runs / configs) - Any expected impacts on model outputs When the MR is approved and tests pass, a maintainer will merge it. Your lpjguess_dave_<your_name> branch remains your main working branch; you do not delete it after merges. 3. Secondary Workflow: Short-Lived Feature or Experiment Branches (For advanced or experimental work.) 3.1. Create a short-lived branch Create a short-lived feature/<topic> branch from either your long-lived branch or lpjguess_dave . Work and commit normally, then open an MR: feature → lpjguess_dave_ , or feature → lpjguess_dave (if ready for direct integration) After merge, delete the feature branch (GitLab can automate this). 4. Where to find Git commands This page intentionally focuses on workflow and review gates. For concrete command sequences, use: Version Control via CLI Version Control via SourceTree

docs.text: Contributing to the Documentation This page explains how to add or update pages on this documentation site. Background The documentation source files are part of the main LPJ-GUESS-DAVE repository (the same repository as the model code), not a separate documentation repo. All documentation changes should therefore be made and reviewed through normal branch + Merge Request workflows in this repository. The docs are organised under docs/ and rendered with MkDocs using mkdocs.yml at the repository root: docs/index.md is the documentation homepage docs/howto/ contains practical how-to guides docs/development/ contains developer-facing and architecture material docs/science/ contains science and model-method documentation mkdocs.yml defines the site navigation and page hierarchy Overview of the Workflow Write or edit a Markdown file under docs/ Preview it locally (in VSCode or with mkdocs serve ) Commit and push to a branch Open a Merge Request on GitLab Once the MR is merged, the site rebuilds automatically Writing in Markdown Documentation pages are plain-text files with a .md extension. Markdown is a lightweight formatting syntax that is readable as-is and renders cleanly in the browser. Prefer Markdown over Word for documentation: It works with version control — diffs, history, and code review all work naturally It renders consistently for every reader without font or layout drift Equations, code blocks, tables, and cross-links are all first-class features No proprietary file format; any text editor works Basic Formatting # Heading 1 ## Heading 2 **bold**, _italic_, `inline code` - bullet item - another item 1. numbered item 2. another item [link text](other-page.md) [external link](https://example.com) ![alt text](../path/to/image.png) For mathematics, see Writing Equations . Code Blocks Fenced code blocks use triple backticks and an optional language identifier for syntax highlighting: ```python def greet(name): return f"Hello, {name}" ``` Admonitions Highlighted callout boxes use the !!! syntax: !!! note This is a note. !!! warning This is a warning. !!! tip This is a tip. Supported types: note , warning , tip , info , danger , success . Tables | Column A | Column B | Column C | |----------|----------|----------| | value 1 | value 2 | value 3 | Previewing Changes Option 1: VSCode Markdown Preview VSCode has a built-in Markdown previewer. Open the .md file and press Ctrl+Shift+V (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+V (macOS) to open a live preview panel beside the editor. This is the quickest way to check formatting while writing, but it does not render MkDocs-specific features (admonitions, math, or the nav sidebar). Option 2: Local Site Preview with mkdocs serve For a full preview that matches what the deployed site looks like, run the development server from the repository root: pip install mkdocs pymdown-extensions mkdocs serve --livereload Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in a browser. The server watches for file changes and reloads automatically — edit and save a .md file to see the result immediately without restarting. Note mkdocs serve requires Python. On Windows, use a terminal where Python is on PATH (e.g. the Anaconda Prompt or a terminal opened from VS Code with a Python environment active). Alternative: Convert a Word Document If content is already written in a Word document ( .docx ), the doc2md script in the docs/ directory can convert it to Markdown using pandoc (you will first need to install pandoc): docs/doc2md input.docx # Creates input.md This handles basic formatting, tables, and equation numbering. Review the output carefully after conversion — Word's equation objects do not translate perfectly, and headings, lists, and figure captions often need manual cleanup. Writing directly in Markdown from the start is generally less work than converting from Word. Adding a New Page Create the .md file under docs/ (e.g. docs/howto/my-topic.md ). Add it to the nav: section of mkdocs.yml : ```yaml How-to: My Topic: howto/my-topic.md ``` Verify it appears correctly with mkdocs serve . Pages not listed under nav: are still built but will not appear in the sidebar navigation. Committing and Raising a Merge Request Once you are happy with your changes: Commit the changed files to a branch (see Version Control via SourceTree or Version Control via CLI ) Push the branch to GitLab Open a Merge Request targeting the lpjguess_dave branch The CI pipeline runs a compile check; the MR can be merged once checks pass Merging to lpjguess_dave triggers the Pages deployment pipeline, which rebuilds and publishes the site automatically within a few minutes No manual deployment step is needed.

docs.text: Running and Debugging via VSCode The repository includes pre-configured VSCode launch and build tasks in .vscode/launch.json and .vscode/tasks.json . These are committed to the repository, so debugging should work without any additional configuration after completing the platform setup. Before You Start VSCode installed with the required extensions (see your platform setup guide: Windows | macOS | Linux ) Climate forcing data downloaded to benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/ (see HIE-Storage ) For the example below, check that this file exists: benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/met/CumberlandPlain.nc If it does not, download the full OzFlux forcing directory before continuing. The OzFlux Site Simulations page explains the input file structure. Run Your First Site Open the repository root folder in VSCode ( File → Open Folder ). Always open the root directory — not a subdirectory such as modules/ or benchmarks/ . Open the Run and Debug panel ( Ctrl+Shift+D on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+D on macOS), or click the debug icon in the left sidebar, or click View -> Run. Select CumberlandPlain from the run-configuration dropdown at the top of the panel. You can select a different OzFlux site later. Press F5 (or the green play button) to start. The pre-launch build task will recompile the model if any source files have changed since the last build. Compilation output appears in the Terminal panel. On Windows and Linux, the model then runs in that terminal, with progress reported there. On macOS, the debugged model's standard output and standard error appear in the Debug Console panel instead; select Debug Console from the panel dropdown at the bottom of VSCode. When the run reaches the end, it prints text like: Simulation completed in 15.05 seconds with 0 errors and 0 warnings. See guess.log for full details The time and counts will differ. FATAL ERROR: followed by Simulation terminated. means the run failed; see Common Failures . Check the Results For Cumberland Plain, outputs are written to: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/out/ The full log is: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/guess.log Open the log if the run failed or reported errors. The exact output files depend on the shared benchmarks/ozflux/outputs.ins configuration; see OzFlux Site Simulations before changing it. Do not commit files in out/ unless a maintainer has asked for them. To run another site, select its configuration from the same dropdown and press F5 . For command-line runs, see Running Serially . Debugger Notes Linux uses gdb ; macOS uses lldb ; Windows uses gdb via MSYS2. The launch configuration selects the correct debugger automatically based on platform. To set a breakpoint: click in the left margin next to a line number in the editor, then press F5 . Execution will pause at that line. The debug console at the bottom of the screen accepts GDB/LLDB commands directly.

docs.text: Choosing Gadi Resources and Estimating Costs This page explains how to choose CPU, memory, and walltime requests for an LPJ-GUESS DAVE job on Gadi and how to estimate its cost. For the submission workflow, see Running on Gadi . Choosing CPU Count and Walltime No single PBS job on Gadi may run for longer than 48 hours . Running a large domain on very few CPUs is therefore not feasible: the job will be killed if it reaches its walltime limit. The shared DAVE environment provides choose_num_cpus.py , which helps choose an efficient CPU count for a given gridcell count and queue: choose_num_cpus.py <total_gridcells> <queue> Adding more CPUs reduces elapsed time for the same approximate SU cost, since billing is per CPU-hour. However, if the gridcell count does not divide evenly across workers, some finish early and sit idle while the slowest worker completes its last gridcell. The script finds a CPU count that minimises that imbalance as well as execution time. Choose a WALLTIME with enough margin for the expected run duration. PBS kills jobs that exceed their requested walltime even when the queue's 48-hour maximum has not been reached. Check the Available Allocation Run nci_account before large jobs to confirm that the project has sufficient allocation remaining. It prints KSU (kilo service unit) usage and availability for your projects: nci_account These helper scripts are available under /scratch/pt17/.bin . If the commands are not found, set up the DAVE shared environment . Estimate a Job Before Submission The qcost helper estimates the SU cost of a PBS job: qcost -c <cpus> -m <memory_GiB> -w <walltime_hours> -q <queue> For example, for 48 CPUs, 192 GiB, two hours, and the normal queue: qcost -c 48 -m 192 -w 2 -q normal Job Charging Gadi charges jobs according to the resources reserved and the walltime used . The general formula is: Job Cost (SU) = Queue Charge Rate × max(NCPUs, Memory Proportion) × Walltime Used (hours) Where: Queue Charge Rate depends on the selected queue; express queues cost more per SU but increase priority. NCPUs is the number of requested CPUs. Memory Proportion is the requested memory divided by the queue's memory-per-core allowance (memory per node divided by CPUs per node). Requesting an outsized amount of memory can therefore increase the cost even if the job does not use it. A job requesting enough memory to fill a node effectively reserves the whole node and is charged accordingly. See the PBS job-cost documentation in the Gadi User Guide for the current queue charge rates and limits. Practical Implications for LPJ-GUESS LPJ-GUESS uses well under 1 GiB of memory per CPU. Its costs are therefore normally dominated by CPU count rather than memory. The normal queue nodes have 48 CPUs and 192 GiB RAM, giving a memory-per-core ratio of 4 GiB/CPU. Because LPJ-GUESS memory use is below this threshold, the billing formula simplifies to: Job Cost (SU) = Queue Charge Rate × NCPUs × Walltime Used Requesting less than 4 GiB per CPU on the normal queue costs the same as requesting 4 GiB per CPU. Request 4 GiB per CPU as a safe default ; it does not cost more and avoids unexpected out-of-memory failures. Estimating LPJ-GUESS Run Cost LPJ-GUESS cost on Gadi is approximately 0.005–0.01 SU per patch . For a run over G gridcells, each containing P patches: estimated SUs ≈ G × P × 0.005 (lower bound) estimated SUs ≈ G × P × 0.01 (upper bound) The cost per SU is approximately $0.04 AUD (indicative—verify against current NCI pricing). These are first-order estimates assuming uniform patch runtime. More productive gridcells (higher biomass turnover) take slightly longer, but the effect is small and choose_num_cpus.py can minimise imbalance across workers. After a job finishes, compare this estimate with the actual cost recorded in the top-level job log. See Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs .

docs.text: This page explains how to choose CPU, memory, and walltime requests for an LPJ-GUESS DAVE job on Gadi and how to estimate its cost. For the submission workflow, see Running on Gadi .

docs.text: No single PBS job on Gadi may run for longer than 48 hours . Running a large domain on very few CPUs is therefore not feasible: the job will be killed if it reaches its walltime limit. The shared DAVE environment provides choose_num_cpus.py , which helps choose an efficient CPU count for a given gridcell count and queue: choose_num_cpus.py <total_gridcells> <queue> Adding more CPUs reduces elapsed time for the same approximate SU cost, since billing is per CPU-hour. However, if the gridcell count does not divide evenly across workers, some finish early and sit idle while the slowest worker completes its last gridcell. The script finds a CPU count that minimises that imbalance as well as execution time. Choose a WALLTIME with enough margin for the expected run duration. PBS kills jobs that exceed their requested walltime even when the queue's 48-hour maximum has not been reached.
docs.title: Choosing CPU Count and Walltime

docs.text: Run nci_account before large jobs to confirm that the project has sufficient allocation remaining. It prints KSU (kilo service unit) usage and availability for your projects: nci_account These helper scripts are available under /scratch/pt17/.bin . docs.text: The qcost helper estimates the SU cost of a PBS job: qcost -c <cpus> -m <memory_GiB> -w <walltime_hours> -q <queue> For example, for 48 CPUs, 192 GiB, two hours, and the normal queue: qcost -c 48 -m 192 -w 2 -q normal

docs.text: Gadi charges jobs according to the resources reserved and the walltime used . Requesting an outsized amount of memory can therefore increase the cost even if the job does not use it. A job requesting enough memory to fill a node effectively reserves the whole node and is charged accordingly. docs.text: Setting Up Gadi Gadi is the HPC system at the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) in Canberra. This page covers the one-time setup and background needed to run LPJ-GUESS DAVE jobs on Gadi. Once your account and environment are ready, continue with Running on Gadi . This guide is not a substitute for the comprehensive Gadi User Guide . Reading at least its sections on PBS, storage, and job debiting before your first run is strongly recommended. Connecting to Gadi ssh <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au Password authentication is possible but requires typing a password on every login, which is inconvenient for repeated sessions or scripted transfers. Setting up an SSH key pair is recommended for day-to-day use. To do this: Generate an ed25519 key pair if you don't already have one (see SSH Key Management ). Register the public key ( id_ed25519.pub ). Log in to Gadi with your password, then append your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. The easiest way is ssh-copy-id (Linux/macOS): ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au You will be prompted for your NCI password once. After that, SSH and SFTP connections will use the key instead. If ssh-copy-id is not available (e.g. on Windows), log in manually and run: mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys << 'EOF' <paste the contents of id_ed25519.pub here> EOF chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Once the key is registered, ssh <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au will connect without a password prompt. Background: PBS Gadi uses PBS Pro (Portable Batch System) as its job scheduler. Rather than running programs directly, you describe the resources your job needs and submit it to PBS, which queues and executes it when resources become available. Concept Description Job A self-contained unit of work submitted via qsub Queue A named pool of compute nodes (e.g. normal , hugemem , express ) Walltime The maximum real-world time a job may run before PBS kills it Service Unit (SU) The unit of compute cost; jobs are billed to a project Project A budget account (e.g. pt17 ) that SUs are charged to Useful PBS commands: Command Description qstat -u $USER List your running and queued jobs qstat -f <jobid> Show detailed status for a specific job qdel <jobid> Cancel a job No single PBS job on Gadi may run for longer than 48 hours. See Choosing Gadi Resources and Estimating Costs for guidance on selecting CPUs, memory, and walltime. Environment Modules Software on Gadi is managed via the environment modules system. Rather than having one global version of each tool, multiple versions coexist and users activate the ones they need: module load netcdf # load the default netcdf version module load gcc/12.1.0 # load a specific version module list # list currently loaded modules module avail netcdf # list available versions of netcdf module show netcdf # show what a module does (paths it sets, etc.) module purge # unload all modules Module consistency The exact module versions loaded when compiling must also be loaded when running . Mismatching MPI implementations between build and runtime is a particularly common and hard-to-diagnose error. The build_gadi and submit_to_gadi.sh scripts ensure consistency; use them rather than loading modules manually. DAVE Shared Environment DAVE helper scripts and custom module files are available to all members of the pt17 group on Gadi. To make them available automatically at login, add this line to your own ~/.bashrc file: source /scratch/pt17/.bin/.bashrc That shared file adds /scratch/pt17/.bin to PATH , making the DAVE helper scripts available as normal shell commands. It also adds the DAVE custom module directory to MODULEPATH , so module avail and module load can see the project-specific modules. One of these modules is lpj-guess-utils , which provides Gadi-compiled versions of standard LPJ-GUESS utilities such as aslice , tslice , and gmap . Many of the shared helper scripts are maintained in the hol430/gadi-scripts repository. After editing ~/.bashrc , either log out and back in, or source it in the current shell: source ~/.bashrc Storage Gadi provides three types of storage, with very different properties. Home Directory ( $HOME ) $HOME ( /home/xxx/<nci_username> ) is limited to 10 GiB . It is intended for configuration files, scripts, and source code— never for job outputs . A run writing even modest output to $HOME will quickly exhaust the quota and cause jobs to fail. Scratch ( /scratch/<project>/$USER ) /scratch is the primary working space for job input and output. It is fast and has a larger quota, but files that have not been accessed or modified for 100 days are automatically deleted without warning. Files are first moved to a quarantine area before permanent deletion. Consult the Gadi User Guide linked above for instructions on listing and recovering quarantined files. No permanent storage The DAVE project does not have permanent storage on Gadi (only scratch). Important results should be backed up to HIE-Storage as soon as possible after a run completes. Gdata ( /g/data/<project> ) /g/data is persistent project storage not subject to the 100-day deletion policy. The DAVE project does not currently have any gdata allocation. PBS Filesystem Access PBS jobs must explicitly declare which filesystems they use, for example: #PBS -l storage=scratch/pt17+gdata/pt17 Accessing an undeclared path fails at runtime even if you can reach it interactively. The submit_to_gadi.sh script handles this automatically for standard runs; only manually written PBS scripts need to consider it. Check Storage Quotas with lquota The shared DAVE environment provides lquota , which prints storage usage and limits for each project you are a member of: lquota

docs.text: Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs This page explains how to check a completed LPJ-GUESS DAVE job on Gadi and diagnose common failures. For building and submitting a job, see Running on Gadi . Start with the Top-level Job Log The main job writes <job name>.log in the run directory. The bottom of this file contains the PBS resource summary, including the resources requested and used and the total job cost in service units (SU). Check this summary after each run, especially if the job took substantially more or less time than expected. As a rough guide, LPJ-GUESS jobs should cost approximately 0.005–0.01 SU per patch , where: total patches = npatch × number of gridcells lower cost estimate = total patches × 0.005 SU upper cost estimate = total patches × 0.01 SU A cost significantly outside this range should be investigated. An unusually high cost may mean that work was duplicated between workers; an unusually low cost may indicate that the run did not process everything expected. See Estimating LPJ-GUESS Run Cost for more detail. Inspect Individual Worker Logs Each worker writes its own log at runs/runX/guess.log , for example runs/run1/guess.log . These logs show which gridcells that worker processed, how long they took, and any warnings or errors encountered. When a run is unexpectedly slow, incomplete, or unusually expensive, compare several worker logs to determine how the work was divided and where time was spent. In particular, if every guess.log lists every gridcell, check for the absolute gridlist path problem . Final Output Files and append.cmd The submission script creates a second PBS job from append.cmd . PBS schedules this job to run after the main job, but only if the main job succeeds. It combines each worker's output files into the final output/ directory. For example: runs/run1/out/lai.out ┐ runs/run2/out/lai.out ├──> output/lai.out runs/run3/out/lai.out ┘ The same process is applied to every output file. If the main job fails, the append job does not run and the individual files remain under runs/runX/out/ for diagnosis or manual recovery. Common Errors Job Takes Much Longer Than Expected One possible cause is that every worker has processed the complete gridlist instead of only its assigned gridcells. The run may otherwise appear to work, so this is easy to miss without checking the job cost and worker logs. The gridlist path must be relative When using submit_to_gadi.sh , never give the gridlist an absolute path in the instruction file. Use ./<gridlist-basename> instead. This is an exception to the general recommendation to use absolute paths for input files. For example, if the gridlist is named gridlist.txt : # Wrong: every worker reads the complete, original gridlist file_gridlist "/scratch/pt17/my/input/gridlist.txt" # Correct: every worker reads its assigned part of the gridlist file_gridlist "./gridlist.txt" The parameter name depends on the input module; for example, it may be file_gridlist or file_gridlist_cf . The same rule applies in either case, and the relative filename must match the basename of the original gridlist. The submission script splits the gridlist between the runs/run1/ ... runs/runN/ directories. During a parallel run, each worker changes into its own directory and should read the split gridlist stored there. An absolute path bypasses that file, causing every worker to process the complete original gridlist. This can multiply the job's cost and cause it to exceed its requested walltime. See Path Considerations for more detail. libnetcdf.so.15: cannot open shared object file Example: /home/590/am8995/code/lpjg_aaron/build/guess: error while loading shared libraries: libnetcdf.so.15: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory This means the executable was compiled against a NetCDF library that is not available in the environment where the model is being run. The most common cause is forgetting to load the netcdf module before running. It can also happen if the model was compiled with one NetCDF module version but run with a different one. Fix: Use ./build_gadi to compile the model. It loads the required Gadi modules, including the default netcdf module. Submit runs with submit_to_gadi.sh , which generates a PBS script that loads the same kind of runtime environment before launching guess . If running manually for a quick test, load NetCDF first: bash module purge module load openmpi gcc cmake netcdf ./build/guess -input nc /path/to/simulation.ins If the error persists, check which modules are loaded in the job output: module list Then rebuild and rerun in a clean, consistent environment: module purge ./build_gadi submit_to_gadi.sh: command not found The DAVE helper scripts are probably not on your PATH . Add the shared DAVE startup file to ~/.bashrc as described in DAVE Shared Environment , then log out and back in or run: source ~/.bashrc Paths Containing ~ Do Not Work in the Configuration File The submission script reads paths from the configuration file literally. Use ${HOME} or a full path instead of ~ : BINARY=${HOME}/lpj-guess-dave/build/guess Job Starts but Cannot Read or Write Files First check that input and output paths exist and are on a filesystem available to the PBS job. Use /scratch/<project>/$USER for run outputs, not $HOME . If you wrote your own PBS script, make sure it declares the filesystems it uses, for example: #PBS -l storage=scratch/pt17 The submit_to_gadi.sh script handles this for standard runs. See Storage for more detail. Job Stops Near the Requested Walltime PBS kills jobs that exceed their walltime request. Gadi also has a maximum 48-hour walltime for a single job. Increase NPROCESS so the run finishes sooner, increase WALLTIME if it was set too low, or split the simulation into smaller jobs. See Choosing CPU Count and Walltime .

docs.text: Version Control via the Command Line This page covers the Git workflow for contributing to LPJ-GUESS DAVE using the terminal. It assumes familiarity with basic Git concepts (commits, branches, remotes). For a gentler introduction, see Version Control via SourceTree . Clone the Repository git clone git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git lpj-guess-dave cd lpj-guess-dave The default branch after cloning is lpjguess_dave . Create a Branch Always work on a dedicated branch, not directly on lpjguess_dave : git switch -c my-feature-branch Use a short, descriptive name with hyphens (e.g. fix-canopy-conductance , add-thome-docs ). Check Status and Review Changes git status # which files have changed git diff # unstaged changes (line-by-line) git diff --staged # changes already staged for commit Stage and Commit Stage specific files you want to include in the next commit: git add path/to/changed/file.cpp path/to/file2.h git add docs/howto/my-page.md Or stage everything in the working tree (use with care): git add -A # stage all changes in the repository, including deletions git add . # stage all changes in the current directory and subdirectories git add -p # interactive patch staging — recommended over git add . Then commit with a message that describes what changed and why: git commit -m "Fix negative VPD crash when RH input is 1.0" Good commit messages use the imperative present tense and explain why the change was made, not just which files were touched. Push the Branch git push -u origin my-feature-branch The -u flag sets the upstream tracking reference so that subsequent git push and git pull calls on this branch need no arguments. Bring a Branch Up to Date Two common workflows are covered below: Bring a long-lived development branch up to date with origin/lpjguess_dave . Pull commits you made to the same branch from another machine. In both workflows, commit or stash local uncommitted changes first. Workflow A: Update from lpjguess_dave (Rebase Recommended) From your development branch: git fetch origin git rebase origin/lpjguess_dave If conflicts occur, resolve them and continue: git add <resolved-file> git rebase --continue If you already pushed the branch earlier, rebase rewrites commit hashes, so you may need: git push --force-with-lease Workflow A (Alternative): Update from lpjguess_dave with Merge If you do not want to rewrite branch history: git fetch origin git merge origin/lpjguess_dave If conflicts occur, resolve them and continue: git add <resolved-file> git merge --continue If your Git version does not support git merge --continue , complete the merge with: git commit Workflow B: Pull Your Own Branch Changes from Another Machine If you pushed commits from machine A and now want them on machine B: git switch my-feature-branch git pull This works because the branch tracks origin/my-feature-branch (set when you first used git push -u origin my-feature-branch ). Rebase vs Merge (What’s the Difference?) rebase replays your branch commits on top of the latest origin/lpjguess_dave , producing a linear history. merge creates a merge commit that ties both histories together, preserving the exact original branch timeline. Practical guidance: Prefer rebase for a clean, linear feature branch history before opening an MR. Prefer merge when you want to avoid history rewriting, especially on shared branches. Avoid rebasing commits that others have already based work on. Open a Merge Request After pushing, open the repository in your browser on GitLab. GitLab will show a banner prompting you to create a Merge Request for the branch you just pushed. Set Target branch to lpjguess_dave . Alternatively, GitLab prints a direct MR creation link in the output of git push : remote: To create a merge request for my-feature-branch, visit: remote: https://gitlab.com/.../merge_requests/new?merge_request[source_branch]=my-feature-branch The CI pipeline runs automatically. The MR can be merged once the pipeline passes and a reviewer has approved it. Note Subsequent pushes to the same branch update the open MR automatically — no need to open a new one. docs.text: HIE-Storage HIE-Storage is a file server used by the DAVE team to store climate forcing data and other large datasets. Connection Details Parameter Value Host hie-storage.sstars.ws Protocol SFTP Authentication SSH key only (password authentication is disabled) Username u<staff_id> — e.g. u123456 If you do not have an account, contact Drew. SSH Key Requirements Password authentication is disabled. You must use an SSH key. ed25519 keys are recommended — RSA keys are rejected as insecure. If you do not have an SSH key yet, or need to create an ed25519 key, see SSH Key Management . Accessing Files There are two ways documented in this wiki to transfer files to and from HIE-Storage: SFTP via FileZilla — graphical client, suitable for browsing and downloading individual files or directories. SFTP via terminal — command-line access, useful for scripted transfers and working on remote systems. OzFlux Forcing Data The climate forcing data required for OzFlux site simulations is at: /data/hiestorage/WorkingData/MEDLYN_GROUP/PROJECTS/dynamics_simulations/lpj-guess/forcing/ozflux/processed This directory should be downloaded and placed at benchmarks/ozflux/forcing inside the repository. See OzFlux Site Simulations for the expected directory structure.

Writing Equations in Markdown This page is a practical reference for writing mathematical equations on this documentation site. If you are familiar with Word's equation editor but new to LaTeX, start here. Equations are written in LaTeX syntax, which is the standard for typesetting mathematics in scientific publishing. The site renders them automatically wherever you write them. Inline vs Display Equations There are two ways to include an equation: Type Syntax When to use Inline $...$ Part of a sentence, e.g. "where \(x\) is…" Display $$...$$ Standalone, centred equation on its own line Inline example — the source: The leaf area index $L$ is the one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground area (m² m⁻²). renders as: The leaf area index \(L\) is the one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground area (m² m⁻²). Display example — the source: $$ E = mc^2 $$ renders as: \[ E = mc^2 \] Tip Use display equations for anything that has multiple terms, fractions, or needs to be easy to refer to. docs.text: Migrating from the Old Upstream LPJ-GUESS Repository This is for people who previously worked on the original/core LPJ-GUESS repo and want to repoint their existing local clone to this new Australian team fork. If you’re cloning fresh, skip this section. 1. Check current remote git remote -v You’ll likely see something like: origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:lpj-guess-developers/LPJ-GUESS.git (fetch) origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:lpj-guess-developers/LPJ-GUESS.git (push) 2. Commit any local work Make sure no work is lost: git status If you see uncommitted changes: git add <files> git commit -m "Save work before migration" 3. Point origin to the new team fork Replace the URL below with the actual team fork URL: git remote set-url origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Verify: git remote -v We intentionally do not keep a remote pointing to the old upstream, to avoid accidental pushes. 4. Push your branches to the new fork List local branches: git branch Push each branch you care about: git checkout <branch-name> git push -u origin <branch-name> 5. Rename your long-lived branch (optional but recommended) If your main working branch was not named lpjguess_dave_<your_name> : git checkout <old-branch> git branch -m lpjguess_dave_<your_name> git push -u origin lpjguess_dave_<your_name> git push origin --delete <old-branch> # optional Ask a maintainer before deleting branches on the remote. 6. Final checks git fetch , git pull , and git push should work normally. git branch -a should show: lpjguess_dave trunk your lpjguess_dave_<name> branch At this point, you’re fully migrated and can follow the primary workflow in Contributing Code (Workflow) . If you have improvements to suggest, please open an Issue titled: “Update CONTRIBUTING / migration docs”
